title: Hosted API demo - chat/text generation basics (streaming, params, retries)
summary: AE + SE demo of Redwood hosted API focused on chat/text generation: streaming behavior, key parameters (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), retry semantics and idempotency, cost/latency tradeoffs, and monitoring in Console. Customer concerned about PHI, SOC2/KMS, and predictable latency for patient-facing use cases. Agreed next steps: send security docs, pricing estimate, and run a small benchmark POC with customer prompts.
topics: Model params: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences
Latency vs cost tradeoffs and batching
Security: SOC 2, encryption, data retention, VPC options
transcript: [00:00] Maya Thompson: Alright, hi everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account. We have Diego from the SE team with me. Quick intros?
[00:12] Lena Park: Hi, Lena here, head of product at Sunrise Medical. We're mostly interested in adding a chat assistant into our patient portal, low latency and strict PHI controls.
[00:22] Samir Patel: Samir, CTO. Main questions around latency, cost, and compliance. We have an internal BERT service but want generation for triage messages.

[00:34] Diego Ruiz: Great, thanks. Today we'll walk through the hosted API for chat/text gen basics — streaming behavior, key parameters you tune, and how retries work. I'll demo the Console a bit so you can see cost/latency metrics live.
[00:48] Julia Kim: quick q — do you support streaming partial tokens? We want incremental display in the UI.

[00:55] Diego Ruiz: Yes, we stream tokens; it's via chunked responses / SSE depending on your client. So you get token-level pieces as they generate which helps perceived latency. There can be slight reordering in corners, but generally it's stable.
[01:15] Lena Park: And can we control how often chunks flush? Like for short answers we want immediate, for long ones we might buffer.

[01:24] Diego Ruiz: You can control some of that server-side with the chunk size and client-side with buffering. For hosted API we expose streaming by default, and you can set max_tokens and also early stop sequences so it doesn't keep going.

[01:42] Maya Thompson: I'll jump in on params — typical ones: temperature (randomness), top_p (nucleus sampling), max_tokens, stop sequences, and also presence/ frequency penalties. For deterministic responses we recommend low temperature and explicit stop sequences.
[01:58] Julia Kim: what's the default max_tokens?
[02:01] Diego Ruiz: Default depends on model; we recommend setting an explicit max_tokens for production. For chat flows, also pass in token_budget so you can bound cost.
[02:14] Samir Patel: On retries: if a request fails mid-generation, what's your recommended client pattern? We can't double-charge or double-send PHI.

[02:24] Diego Ruiz: Good question. We provide idempotency keys you can set per user-turn. If the client retries with same idempotency key, the server recognizes duplicate and will return the previous result or indicate it failed. Also we recommend exponential backoff for transient errors.

[02:41] Maya Thompson: We also surfaced retry behaviors in SDKs — built-in retry middleware that respects idempotency headers. For non-idempotent actions you should store partial state client-side before confirming to avoid duplication.
[02:55] Lena Park: Is there a limit on idempotency key retention? Like how long does Redwood keep the mapping?
[03:02] Diego Ruiz: We retain recent idempotency mappings for a configurable window, typically 24 to 72 hours depending on account plan — we can share the exact policy in the security docs.
[03:13] Julia Kim: On billing — is cost per token and do streaming tokens count as full tokens?

[03:18] Maya Thompson: Billing is per output token and input tokens; streaming doesn't create extra billing — it's just transparent delivery of the same tokens. The Console shows token breakdown per request so you can see chargeable units.
[03:32] Samir Patel: latency targets — can you hit sub-300ms for short responses?

[03:37] Diego Ruiz: Depends on model and sequence length. For small prompts on optimized runtime we routinely see <200ms p95 on our hosted tiers for base models. Larger context or longer generations push that out. Also batching can increase throughput but adds latency; you can configure a low-latency route for patient-facing calls.
[03:57] Lena Park: That low-latency route — is that part of Redwood Dedicated or hosted can do it too?

[04:03] Diego Ruiz: Hosted supports tiered performance routes. For predictable p95 we often recommend Dedicated, but for many customers hosted low-latency SLOs meet their needs — it's a tradeoff with cost.
[04:14] Maya Thompson: I'll show the Console now — Diego, if you want to pull up a live demo request?
[04:20] Diego Ruiz: Yep, demoing a sample chat endpoint. Sending a prompt now, streaming on. You should see tokens appear — first chunk at around 200ms.
[04:35] [demo audio spike / brief crosstalk]
[04:40] Diego Ruiz: streaming chunks are coming in — you can see partial output, then finalization. In the Console trace we show per-token latency, cost, and which model/kernel served the request.
[04:57] Lena Park: That trace view is helpful. Can we map traces to our user IDs for audit? We need full traceability for compliance.

[05:06] Diego Ruiz: Yes, you can send a request_id or external_user_id metadata which gets stored in logs and shows up in traces. With Private/VPC deployments you can also configure stricter retention and export logs to your SIEM.
[05:20] Samir Patel: About PHI: do you have SOC 2 and can we have dedicated keys?

[05:25] Maya Thompson: We are SOC 2 compliant. For encryption we integrate with customer KMS (bring-your-own-key) for Dedicated/Private, and hosted has envelope encryption with customer-managed KMS on enterprise plans. We'll attach SOC2 and KMS docs.
[05:40] Julia Kim: Any on-prem option if we need air-gapped?
[05:43] Diego Ruiz: Yes, Redwood Private supports on-prem and VPC packages for regulated workloads. That's a longer engagement but supported.
[05:53] Lena Park: Back to retries — if the stream cuts mid-response, is there a way to resume from token N?

[05:59] Diego Ruiz: Not resume per se; our pattern is to store the last response and replay the prompt with an idempotency key. For large completions, we recommend chunked checkpoints on the client to resume UX while the server returns the final or cached response.
[06:18] Maya Thompson: Also note we have prefix caching and KV cache optimization for chat workloads — that reduces repeated computation for the same context which helps both latency and cost.
[06:28] Samir Patel: How does batching interact with streaming?

[06:31] Diego Ruiz: Batching trades latency for throughput. Streaming while batching is possible but increases the time until first token. For patient UI we recommend minimal batching on that route; use batching for async background jobs.
[06:44] Julia Kim: Do you expose model selection in the API? We want to fall back to a cheaper model under high load.

[06:50] Diego Ruiz: Yes, model parameter is part of the request. We support smart routing rules to fallback to compatible model variants automatically when capacity is constrained. You can configure cost-latency routing policies.
[07:05] Lena Park: Can we set per-route quotas or rate limits?
[07:09] Maya Thompson: Yes, per-route quotas, rate limits, and token budgets are configurable via the Console. You can also create per-team API keys with RBAC.
[07:18] Samir Patel: For the POC, what's the fastest way to evaluate latency under our prompts?

[07:23] Diego Ruiz: Send us a representative prompt set and traffic profile. We can run a short benchmark on hosted with telemetry and share results; for heavier guarantees we recommend a Dedicated pilot.
[07:34] Maya Thompson: I'll capture that as an action — Diego will run the benchmark once we get prompts.
[07:40] [10 min demo interlude with sample prompts and live Console metrics — audio muted in transcript]
[17:45] Diego Ruiz: back to the call — demo showed p50 around 120ms for the short prompts. You can see cost per 1k tokens in the sidebar, and a breakdown of input vs output tokens.
[17:58] Julia Kim: Small correction — in our app we have images and some tabular data. Does Redwood accept structured attachments in prompt?
[18:06] Diego Ruiz: We accept structured input as part of prompt JSON; for larger assets we recommend pre-processing into embeddings or summarizing before sending to generation to control token size.
[18:20] Lena Park: Any guardrails for hallucinations? We need medical-safe outputs.

[18:26] Maya Thompson: We provide prompt templates, safety filters, and quality monitoring. You can set automated evals in Redwood Optimize to detect regressions on your test set and alert if hallucination increases.
[18:40] Samir Patel: On logging: how long are transcripts/logs retained by default?
[18:45] Diego Ruiz: Default retention is 90 days for hosted, configurable for enterprise. With Private you control retention and export. We'll include retention options in the security pack.
[18:56] Lena Park: Ok — wrapping up, what's the cost model for a small POC?

[19:02] Maya Thompson: Hosted is usage-based per token. For a POC we can provide credits or a short-term trial to validate latency/quality. If you need reserved throughput we'll propose a short Dedicated commit estimate.
[19:14] Samir Patel: Good. Any blockers on integration? SDKs and example code?
[19:18] Diego Ruiz: We have Python/Node SDKs and sample React streaming components. I'll share links after the call.
[19:27] Lena Park: Great. One more compliance note — we need to know if data is used for training models or persisted for research.
[19:33] Maya Thompson: By default hosted may use telemetry for improving models, but on enterprise plans you can opt out and enable no-training/data-retention flags. We'll put that in the docs.
[19:44] Julia Kim: can you send the SOC2 and the KMS integration guide?
[19:48] Maya Thompson: yes, sending after. Also pricing and sample benchmark plan.
[19:55] Samir Patel: sounds good. timeline wise we're looking to have a POC next 2 weeks if the latency looks right.
[20:02] Maya Thompson: We'll aim to run a hosted benchmark as soon as you send prompts. Diego, add timeline to action items.
[20:07] Diego Ruiz: noted. I'll schedule the benchmark run and share results by next Wednesday.
[20:12] [recap and next steps]

[20:15] Maya Thompson: Recap — Maya to send security docs (SOC2, KMS guide), pricing estimate and sample SDK links; Diego to run benchmark with submitted prompts; Samir/Julia to provide prompt samples and traffic profile. Agreed POC target is two weeks.
[20:34] Lena Park: thanks all, that works. We'll get prompts over by Friday.
[20:38] Maya Thompson: perfect, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with email and a calendar invite for the benchmark sync.
[20:45] call end

Diego — run hosted benchmark with customer prompts and share results by 2026-03-11
